title: Area II review: Preflight Procedures
intro: These questions mix the five ASEL Tasks of Area II: preflight assessment, flight deck management, engine starting, taxiing and the before-takeoff check. Many join two of them on one commercial flight, from the records check to the takeoff clearance.

questions.q: Your tour airplane's 100-hour inspection comes due at 2,310.0 hours. You carry paying passengers until the tach shows 2,309.4, then fly the airplane alone to a shop 1.7 hours away. It arrives at 2,311.1 and gets its 100-hour there. When is the next 100-hour due?
options: 2,411.1 hours
2,409.4 hours
2,410.0 hours
2,420.0 hours
questions.why: The 100-hour limit may be exceeded by not more than 10 hours while en route to a place where the inspection can be done, and that excess time must be counted in the next 100 hours [[60:521|14 CFR 91.409(b)]] [[60:522|14 CFR 91.409(b)]]. Excess: 2,311.1 - 2,310.0 = 1.1 hours. Next due: 2,311.1 + 100 - 1.1 = 2,410.0. 2,411.1 forgets to count the excess, and 2,420.0 treats the 10 hours as a bonus instead of a ferry allowance.

questions.q: A customer books a paid photo flight along a coastline, on a clear day. Part of the route is over water beyond power-off gliding distance from shore. Under 14 CFR 91.205, what must be aboard?
options: Approved flotation gear readily available to each occupant, and at least one pyrotechnic signaling device
Flotation gear for the pilot only, since passengers are not crew
Nothing extra, because this rule applies only to night flights
A life raft for the group, but only under Part 135
questions.why: For a flight for hire over water beyond power-off gliding distance from shore, 91.205(b)(12) requires approved flotation gear readily available to each occupant and, unless operating under Part 121, at least one pyrotechnic signaling device [[60:487|14 CFR 91.205(b)(12)]]. It is in the VFR day list, paragraph (b), so it applies in daylight too; the night list is paragraph (c) [[60:487|14 CFR 91.205(c)]]. The rule says each occupant, so pilot-only flotation does not meet it. The same route flown not for hire would not trigger this item.

questions.q: Your tour airplane has an airworthiness directive that requires a repetitive inspection every 50 hours of time in service. It comes due in 0.4 hours, and your next paid tour lasts 1.0 hour. The annual and 100-hour are both current. What is true?
options: You may fly the tour, because ADs allow up to 10 hours over, like the 100-hour
You may fly it if you note the overrun in the logbook afterward
ADs are advisory for Part 91 airplanes, so the owner decides
You may not overfly the AD's hour limit unless the AD itself allows it, so the inspection comes first
questions.why: ADs are regulatory and must be complied with unless a specific exemption is granted. The PHAK uses this very case, a repetitive inspection every 50 hours, and says there is no provision to overfly an AD's maximum hour requirement unless it is written into the AD [[1:242|PHAK 9-12]]. The 10-hour allowance belongs only to the 100-hour inspection, and only while en route to where it can be done [[60:522|14 CFR 91.409(b)]], so it does not stretch an AD.

questions.q: Checking the records before a charter, you see the ELT transmitter has run for a total of about 70 minutes, from several accidental activations, since its battery was installed. The battery is at 30 percent of its useful life. What does the PHAK say?
options: Nothing yet, because replacement is due only at 50 percent of useful life
Replace or recharge the battery, because the transmitter has been in use for more than 1 cumulative hour
Nothing yet, because only one continuous use of over an hour counts
Replace the whole ELT, because an hour of use means it has failed
questions.why: ELT batteries must be replaced, or recharged if rechargeable, when the transmitter has been in use for more than 1 cumulative hour, or when 50 percent of the battery's useful life has expired [[1:239|PHAK 9-9]]. Either trigger is enough. 70 minutes of total use is more than 60, so the 30 percent useful life does not save it. The rule is about cumulative use, not one continuous run, and it calls for a battery, not a new ELT.

questions.q: Use the figure. Planning a paid tour from a short runway on a hot day, you rate a runway overrun as occasional in likelihood and critical in severity. What does the RMH say about going?
options: Medium (green): go, but mitigate if you can
Serious (yellow): no-go unless you mitigate until a new assessment shows medium or low
High (red): no-go, and no mitigation can change that
Low: go, since only catastrophic outcomes need action
questions.why: Crossing occasional with critical on the matrix gives serious (yellow); the RMH uses this exact runway overrun case as its example [[30:35|RMH 4-2]]. Serious or high means no-go unless you find a way to reduce the risk so the next assessment shows medium or low [[30:35|RMH 4-2]]. Medium (green) is the remote and critical box, one row down. One way to mitigate is to add margins to the performance data [[30:39|RMH 5-1]]. If you are unsure between two levels, use the more conservative one [[30:35|RMH 4-2]].

questions.q: Before an IFR charter you set the current altimeter setting. Field elevation is 1,240 ft and the altimeter reads 1,330 ft. What do you conclude?
options: It is fine, because it is within 100 ft
It is fine; you can adjust it yourself with a small screwdriver, as you would a VSI
It only matters above 18,000 ft, where everyone sets 29.92
It is 90 ft off, more than the 75 ft the AFH allows for IFR, so it is not acceptable for this IFR flight
questions.why: Set to the current altimeter setting, the altimeter should read field elevation within 75 feet for IFR flight [[24:42|AFH 2-5]]. 1,330 - 1,240 = 90 ft, which is outside that. The mechanical VSI is the only flight instrument the pilot may adjust; others need an FAA-certificated repairman or mechanic [[24:42|AFH 2-5]]. There is no 100 ft allowance in the AFH.

questions.q: You plan a night tour from a field with two runways. Which statement about a temporarily closed runway is true?
options: Yellow crosses are placed only at each end of the runway, and there may be no visual sign at all, so check NOTAMs and ATIS
It always has lighted yellow crosses, so you can find out when you get there
White crosses are painted every 1,000 ft along its whole length
Its edge lights are turned off, which is the only sign used
questions.why: A temporarily closed runway has yellow crosses only at each end, or a raised lighted yellow cross may be used instead. But a visual sign may not be present at all, depending on the closure and the airport, so pilots should check NOTAMs and ATIS [[33:161|AIM 2-3-6e]]. That is why the PAVE environment check includes NOTAMs for closed runways and lights out [[1:48|PHAK 2-9]]. A lighted cross is only one option, not a promise, so waiting to see it on arrival is the trap.

questions.q: A parent on your Part 91 tour brings a booster seat for her 5-year-old. It has no marking showing FAA approval. What is the rule?
options: Use it if it is secured to a forward-facing seat with the airplane's belt
Use it only while the parent holds the child on her lap
It is not approved for use in aircraft; the child sits in an approved seat with its own safety belt
Use it if it carries a motor vehicle safety standard label
questions.why: Booster-type child restraints, along with vest- and harness-type ones, are not approved for use in aircraft unless they carry FAA approval markings [[60:442|14 CFR 91.107(a)(3)(iii)(B)(4)]]. So the child uses an approved seat with the belt secured during surface movement, takeoff and landing [[60:441|14 CFR 91.107(a)(3)]]. A lap hold is only for a child who has not reached the second birthday and uses no restraining device [[60:441|14 CFR 91.107(a)(3)(i)]]. A motor vehicle label alone does not override the booster exclusion.

questions.q: After the last tour of the night you pull the mixture to cutoff, turn off the avionics and the master, and step out to help the passengers, leaving the ignition key on BOTH. A line worker starts to push the airplane back by its propeller. What is the hazard?
options: None, because with the master off there is no power for the spark plugs
Only the starter could engage, and it needs the key in START
The battery could slowly drain through the magnetos
The engine can fire if the propeller moves, because magnetos need no outside electrical power
questions.why: After shutdown, turn the ignition switch OFF. Even with the battery and master switches OFF, the engine can fire and turn over if the ignition is left ON and the propeller is moved, because the magneto needs no outside source of electrical power [[1:176|PHAK 7-16]]. Magnetos are completely independent of the airplane's electrical system [[1:175|PHAK 7-15]], so the master switch protects no one. Whenever anyone touches a propeller, assume the ignition is on [[24:53|AFH 2-16]]. Your assessment lasts until the airplane is secured [[24:38|AFH 2-1]].

questions.q: Your new employer's SOP says: "Run the Before Takeoff checklist sometime during taxi, when convenient." What weakness does AC 120-71B point out?
options: None, because flexible timing lowers workload
A floating start creates a high risk of starting late and rushing, or never starting it; tie it to a clear event, such as a set point before the hold-short line
Checklists should be done from memory once a pilot is experienced
The checklist belongs after the takeoff clearance, not before
questions.why: AC 120-71B says a checklist start is best anchored to a clear cue, such as reaching a point 2,000 feet before the hold-short line. "Floating" starts, left open to any time during taxi, create a high risk of starting late and rushing, or not starting at all [[59:18|AC 120-71B 5.1.5]]. Doing a checklist while taxiing is itself high risk, because you can't give full attention to both [[59:18|AC 120-71B 5.1.3]]. For one pilot, AC 91-73B adds: run checklists stopped, or taxiing straight with no complex intersections [[7:4|AC 91-73B 7b(2)(a)]]. Flexible timing feels easier, but it is the trap.

questions.q: Climbing on autopilot to an assigned 6,000 ft, you armed altitude capture. Passing 6,100 ft, the mode annunciator still shows vertical speed active, with the altitude mode only armed. What do the sources say?
options: Nothing is wrong; armed modes always engage on their own
Reprogram the flight plan first, then fix the altitude
Armed modes must be verified as they engage; it did not capture, so act now, for example with altitude hold or by hand flying back to 6,000 ft
Wait; an armed mode often captures a few hundred feet late
questions.why: Managing the autopilot means knowing which modes are engaged and which are armed, verifying that armed functions such as altitude capture engage at the right time, and acting promptly when the system does not do what you expect [[1:70|PHAK 2-31]]. The annunciator is the source for who is doing what, and armed-to-active changes can hide an error until later [[59:29|AC 120-71B 6.9.1.1]] [[59:29|AC 120-71B 6.9.2]]. Reprogramming first leaves the path uncontrolled; a lower level of automation keeps the flight path in hand while you sort it out [[30:51|RMH 7-2]].

questions.q: You fly a company single with a second pilot as pilot monitoring. Ground has cleared you to the runway. The PM wants to read the Before Takeoff checklist while you taxi, and you want to load the departure into the GPS at the same time. What fits FAA guidance?
options: Only one pilot should be head-down while the airplane moves; better, load the GPS before taxi and run the checklist stopped or on a straight taxiway
Do both at once so you are ready at the hold line
You, the taxiing pilot, read the checklist while the PM watches outside
Skip the checklist; the flow you did before taxi is enough
questions.why: With two pilots, only one should be head-down at any time the airplane is in motion [[59:19|AC 120-71B 5.2.2.1]]. GPS entries belong before the first taxi [[7:4|AC 91-73B 7b(2)(g)]], and pre-departure checklists are best done stopped or taxiing straight ahead with no complex intersections [[7:4|AC 91-73B 7b(2)(a)]]. A flow does not replace the checklist: you do the flow, then use the checklist to confirm it [[59:17|AC 120-71B 5.1.2]]. Having the taxiing pilot read puts the wrong person head-down.

questions.q: Taxiing to the run-up area on a paid tour, you notice a back-seat passenger has unbuckled to reach a camera bag. What do the rules say?
options: Each person must occupy an approved seat with the belt fastened during movement on the surface, so have the passenger buckle up
It is allowed, because belts are required only for takeoff and landing
It is allowed at a nontowered airport
Only the front-seat occupants must stay belted during taxi
questions.why: Each person on board must occupy an approved seat with the safety belt, and shoulder harness if installed, secured during movement on the surface, takeoff and landing [[60:441|14 CFR 91.107(a)(3)]]. Before moving on the surface you, the PIC, must make sure each person was told to fasten it [[60:441|14 CFR 91.107(a)(2)]]. The rule covers every seat and every airport.

questions.q: Your older airplane has a generator, not an alternator. Right after start at 1,000 rpm, the ammeter sits a little on the minus side. At run-up rpm it moves to the plus side. What does this show?
options: A failing generator, so cancel the flight
A voltage regulator failure
Normal for a generator: at low rpm it may not carry the whole load, so the battery helps, and at higher rpm it charges the battery
A starter still engaged after the start
questions.why: Most DC generators don't make enough current at low engine rpm to run the whole electrical system, so the battery carries the load and can be drained quickly [[1:190|PHAK 7-30]]. On the ammeter, minus means more current drawn than replaced, and plus shows the battery charging. A full-scale minus deflection would mean a generator malfunction, and full-scale plus a regulator problem [[1:191|PHAK 7-31]]. A stuck starter shows as a high ammeter or loadmeter reading, low voltage, dim lights or radio noise [[18:1|AC 91-55A para 6]], not a small minus that clears with rpm.

questions.q: At the run-up, switching from BOTH to RIGHT gives no rpm drop at all, while LEFT gives a normal small drop. While you wait for a mechanic, a line worker wants to turn the propeller by hand to move the airplane. What is true?
options: No drop means the right magneto is perfect, so fly
No drop is not normal, so don't fly; and anyone touching the propeller should assume the ignition is on
Don't fly, but the propeller is safe to move once the key is OFF
Recheck at full throttle; if there is still no drop, the check passed
questions.why: A small drop on each magneto is normal; the PHAK says no drop is not normal and the airplane should not be flown [[1:175|PHAK 7-15]] [[1:176|PHAK 7-16]]. Turning the key OFF does not make the propeller safe. A faulty switch can sit at OFF and still let the engine start [[24:53|AFH 2-16]], and a broken magneto ground wire can let it start when the propeller is moved [[1:176|PHAK 7-16]]. So always assume the ignition is on [[24:53|AFH 2-16]].

questions.q: You make a night departure from a towered airport. Which lighting plan fits the AFH, AC 91-73B and the AIM?
options: Beacon on only once cleared for takeoff; landing light on for the whole taxi
Anticollision lights at start and nav lights for taxi, but landing lights on as soon as you enter the runway to line up and wait
Strobes on for the whole taxi, even if they glare at other pilots

Before start, anticollision and position lights; before taxi, navigation, position and anticollision lights, with the taxi light while moving; crossing a runway, all exterior lights; line up and wait, all but landing lights; landing lights with the takeoff clearance
questions.why: Anticollision lights go on before engine start, and at night the position lights too [[24:53|AFH 2-16]]. Before taxi: navigation, position and anticollision lights, and the taxi light while moving; all exterior lights to cross a runway; all lights except landing lights to enter the runway or line up and wait; landing lights when cleared for takeoff [[7:10|AC 91-73B 7h(2)]] [[33:266|AIM 4-3-24]]. Turning landing lights on in line up and wait is the tempting error. Strobes stay off on the ground if they affect others' vision [[33:266|AIM 4-3-24e]].

questions.q: Leaving the FBO ramp at a towered airport, you reach two yellow lines across the pavement: one solid, on your side, and one dashed, on the far side. What does this marking mean?
options: A runway holding position; hold until cleared onto the runway
A taxiway/taxiway holding position
A taxiway edge; the pavement beyond is not for aircraft
The edge of the movement area; past the dashed line you are in the area under ATC, so have a ground clearance before you cross
questions.why: The nonmovement area boundary is one solid and one dashed yellow line. The solid line is on the nonmovement side and the dashed line on the movement area side, the area under ATC [[33:159|AIM 2-3-6c]]. At an airport with an operating tower you need a clearance to operate on a taxiway [[60:454|14 CFR 91.129(i)]]. A runway holding position marking has four yellow lines, two solid and two dashed [[33:151|AIM 2-3-5a]], and a taxiway/taxiway hold is a single dashed line [[33:151|AIM 2-3-5c]].

questions.q: Just after you start rolling out of parking, you retard the throttle and test each brake. The left pedal goes soft and the airplane barely slows. What does the AFH say to do?
options: Shut the engine down immediately
Keep going slowly and steer with rudder, since brakes are not needed for taxi
Pump the pedal and taxi to the run-up area to recheck
Use the right brake and differential power to steer
questions.why: Test the brakes as soon as the airplane is moving: a little power, then throttle back and a little pressure on one brake, then the other. If braking performance is unsatisfactory, shut the engine down immediately [[24:56|AFH 2-19]]. Taxiing on with rudder alone gives up the ability to stop where and when you need to, which the AFH lists among the primary requirements for safe taxiing [[24:56|AFH 2-19]].

questions.q: Ground clears you to Runway 27 via Alpha. Your numbers show you could depart from the Alpha 3 intersection, halfway down, but you did not ask ground for it. What is expected?
options: Line up at Alpha 3, since your numbers work
Hold short at Alpha 3 and call tower, since intersections need no approval
Taxi to, but not onto, the end of Runway 27; if you want Alpha 3, get ground's approval first, and state your position when you call tower
Ask tower for the distance from Alpha 3 to the ends of the declared distances
questions.why: An aircraft is expected to taxi to, but not onto, the end of the assigned runway unless ground control approved an intersection departure, and you should state your position when calling the tower from an intersection [[33:253|AIM 4-3-10d]] [[33:253|AIM 4-3-10e]]. Before accepting one, your required takeoff distance must fit the reduced runway length and reduced declared distances [[33:253|AIM 4-3-10b]]. Controllers give the distance to the runway end on request, but they cannot give the distance to the ends of the declared distances [[33:253|AIM 4-3-10c]].

questions.q: Arriving on a paid flight in light rain, Tower says: "Cleared to land Runway 27, hold short of Runway 36." The ALD looks just long enough for a dry runway. What fits the sources?
options: Accept, because the weather is above 1,000 ft and 3 miles
Decline and ask for full length; the PHAK says LAHSO is not authorized on wet runways, and the PIC may always decline
Accept, and use the full runway later if you need it
Accept with "wilco" and plan to decide on rollout
questions.why: The PHAK lists LAHSO as not authorized on wet runways [[1:345|PHAK 14-11]]. The AIM gives the PIC final authority to accept or decline and expects a decline when it would compromise safety [[33:254|AIM 4-3-11b3]]. Once accepted, a LAHSO clearance must be followed unless amended or in an emergency, though you may still go around [[33:255|AIM 4-3-11b5]], so accepting now and using the full runway later is not an option. The 1,000 ft and 3 mile minimum is only the weather ATC needs to offer it [[33:256|AIM 4-3-11c5]], not proof that it fits your airplane.

questions.q: Taxiing in thick fog at a large airport, you become unsure whether you have passed your turn onto Taxiway Kilo. You can't see the tower. What does the AIM say?
options: Keep going; the tower is watching and will warn you
Tell the controller at the first sign you are disoriented, because the tower may not be able to see you
Turn onto the next taxiway that looks right, then confirm
Do the Before Takeoff checklist now while you work it out
questions.why: In low visibility the tower may not be able to see aircraft on the airport, so no one may be confirming you follow your instructions. Notify the controller at the first sign of becoming disoriented [[33:262|AIM 4-3-19a]] [[33:262|AIM 4-3-19b]]. Checklists and nonessential talk wait until you are stopped with the brakes set [[33:262|AIM 4-3-19d]]. You can also ask for progressive taxi [[33:261|AIM 4-3-18b3]]. Picking the taxiway that looks right is expectation bias at work [[30:45|RMH 6-2]].

questions.q: The POH zero-wind takeoff distance is 1,800 ft. Tower offers Runway 9 with a 6-knot tailwind, and your lift-off speed is 60 knots. Using the PHAK rule of thumb, about what takeoff distance should you expect?
options: About 1,460 ft
About 1,980 ft
About 2,180 ft
About 1,800 ft, since a light tailwind does not matter
questions.why: 6 / 60 = 10 percent of takeoff speed. A tailwind of 10 percent of takeoff airspeed increases takeoff distance about 21 percent [[1:271|PHAK 11-15]]: 1,800 x 1.21 = 2,178, about 2,180 ft. 1,460 ft (1,800 x 0.81) is the headwind case, about 19 percent shorter. 1,980 ft is a plain 10 percent guess. Compare the result with the runway available before you accept [[60:440|14 CFR 91.103]].

questions.q: In a small airplane you are holding at an intersection 2,000 ft down Runway 27. A Boeing 757 has just taken off from the runway end. You would like to go right away. What applies?
options: Ask for a waiver of the 3-minute interval, and ATC can then clear you
No interval applies, because a 757 is not a heavy
A 2-minute wait is enough, the same as after a low approach
A 3-minute interval is mandatory for a small airplane behind a B757, so you wait
questions.why: The waiver request in AIM 4-3-10f covers small aircraft behind a large nonheavy aircraft, and the AIM leaves the B757 out of it [[33:253|AIM 4-3-10f]]. For small aircraft behind a B757, the 3-minute interval is mandatory [[33:253|AIM 4-3-10h]]. The 2-minute wait is for a larger aircraft's low approach, missed approach or touch-and-go [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6b8]]. When you do go, rotate before the 757's rotation point and climb above its path [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6b6]].

questions.q: Before takeoff in an airplane with electric trim and an autopilot, which check fits the AFH?
options: Run the trim nose-up and nose-down, confirm the trim disconnect works, set takeoff trim, and finish the autopilot's computer and trim checks before you engage it
Engage the autopilot first, then let it run its self-test in flight
Check only that the trim indicator shows takeoff, since testing the switch could cause a runaway
Skip the disconnect check if the trim circuit breaker is in
questions.why: The AFH has you actuate the trim switch both ways, verify the trim disconnect (if equipped) works, then set takeoff trim [[24:344|AFH 17-10]]. All flight director and autopilot computer and trim checks come before engagement, and many systems need a self-test first [[24:257|AFH 13-8]]. For a trim runaway you press the disconnect or pull the trim circuit breaker [[24:348|AFH 17-14]], so you need to know both work and where they are. A breaker that is in tells you nothing about the disconnect.
